{{Short description|Topological relational characteristic}}
{{One source|date=May 2025}}

{{Separation axioms}}
In [[topology]], two points of a [[topological space]] ''X'' are '''topologically indistinguishable'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Math 535 - General Topology |url=https://uregina.ca/~franklam/Math535/Math535_HW6_1003.pdf |website=uregina.ca |access-date=19 May 2025}}</ref> if they have exactly the same [[neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]]s. That is, if ''x'' and ''y'' are points in ''X'', and ''N<sub>x</sub>'' is the set of all neighborhoods that contain ''x'', and ''N<sub>y</sub>'' is the set of all neighborhoods that contain ''y'', then ''x'' and ''y'' are "topologically indistinguishable" [[if and only if]]&nbsp;''N<sub>x</sub>''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''N<sub>y</sub>''.
(See Hausdorff's axiomatic [[Characterizations of the category of topological spaces|neighborhood systems]].)

Intuitively, two points are topologically indistinguishable if the topology of ''X'' is unable to discern between the points.

Two points of ''X'' are '''topologically distinguishable''' if they are not topologically indistinguishable. This means there is an [[open set]] containing precisely one of the two points (equivalently, there is a [[closed set]] containing precisely one of the two points). This open set can then be used to distinguish between the two points. A [[T0 space|T<sub>0</sub> space]] is a topological space in which every pair of distinct points is topologically distinguishable. This is the weakest of the [[separation axiom]]s.

Topological indistinguishability defines an [[equivalence relation]] on any topological space ''X''. If ''x'' and ''y'' are points of ''X'' we write ''x'' ≡ ''y'' for "''x'' and ''y'' are topologically indistinguishable". The [[equivalence class]] of ''x'' will be denoted by [''x''].

==Examples==

By definition, any two distinct points in a [[T0 space|T<sub>0</sub> space]] are topologically distinguishable. On the other hand, [[Regular space|regularity]] and [[Normal space|normality]] do not imply T<sub>0</sub>, so we can find nontrivial examples of topologically indistinguishable points in regular or normal topological spaces. In fact, almost all of the examples given below are [[completely regular]].

*In an [[indiscrete space]], any two points are topologically indistinguishable.
*In a [[pseudometric space]], two points are topologically indistinguishable if and only if the distance between them is zero.
*In a [[seminormed vector space]], ''x'' ≡ ''y'' if and only if ‖''x'' &minus; ''y''‖ = 0.
**For example, let ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''') be the space of all [[measurable function]]s from '''R''' to '''R''' which are [[square integrable]] (see [[Lp space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup> space]]). Then two functions ''f'' and ''g'' in ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''') are topologically indistinguishable if and only if they are equal [[almost everywhere]].
*In a [[topological group]], ''x'' ≡ ''y'' if and only if ''x''<sup>&minus;1</sup>''y'' ∈ cl{''e''} where cl{''e''} is the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of the [[trivial subgroup]]. The equivalence classes are just the [[coset]]s of cl{''e''} (which is always a [[normal subgroup]]).
*[[Uniform space]]s generalize both pseudometric spaces and topological groups. In a uniform space, ''x'' ≡ ''y'' if and only if the pair (''x'', ''y'') belongs to every [[entourage (topology)|entourage]]. The intersection of all the entourages is an equivalence relation on ''X'' which is just that of topological indistinguishability.
*Let ''X'' have the [[initial topology]] with respect to a family of functions <math>\{f_\alpha : X \to Y_\alpha\}</math>. Then two points ''x'' and ''y'' in ''X'' will be topologically indistinguishable if the family <math>f_\alpha</math> does not separate them (i.e. <math>f_\alpha(x) = f_\alpha(y)</math> for all <math>\alpha</math>).
*Given any equivalence relation on a set ''X'' there is a topology on ''X'' for which the notion of topological indistinguishability agrees with the given equivalence relation. One can simply take the equivalence classes as a [[base (topology)|base]] for the topology. This is called the [[partition topology]] on ''X''.

==Specialization preorder==

The topological indistinguishability relation on a space ''X'' can be recovered from a natural [[preorder]] on ''X'' called the [[specialization preorder]]. For points ''x'' and ''y'' in ''X'' this preorder is defined by
:''x'' &le; ''y'' [[if and only if]] ''x'' &isin; cl{''y''}
where cl{''y''} denotes the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of {''y''}. Equivalently, ''x'' ≤ ''y'' if the [[neighborhood system]] of ''x'', denoted ''N''<sub>''x''</sub>, is contained in the neighborhood system of ''y'':
:''x'' &le; ''y'' if and only if ''N''<sub>''x''</sub> &sub; ''N''<sub>''y''</sub>.
It is easy to see that this relation on ''X'' is [[reflexive relation|reflexive]] and [[transitive relation|transitive]] and so defines a preorder. In general, however, this preorder will not be [[antisymmetric relation|antisymmetric]]. Indeed, the equivalence relation determined by ≤ is precisely that of topological indistinguishability:
:''x'' &equiv; ''y'' if and only if ''x'' &le; ''y'' and ''y'' &le; ''x''.

A topological space is said to be [[R0 space|symmetric (or R<sub>0</sub>)]] if the specialization preorder is [[symmetric relation|symmetric]] (i.e. ''x'' ≤ ''y'' implies ''y'' ≤ ''x''). In this case, the relations ≤ and ≡ are identical. Topological indistinguishability is better behaved in these spaces and easier to understand. Note that this class of spaces includes all [[regular space|regular]] and [[completely regular space]]s.

==Properties==

===Equivalent conditions===

There are several equivalent ways of determining when two points are topologically indistinguishable. Let ''X'' be a topological space and let ''x'' and ''y'' be points of ''X''. Denote the respective [[closure (topology)|closure]]s of ''x'' and ''y'' by cl{''x''} and cl{''y''}, and the respective [[neighborhood system]]s by ''N''<sub>''x''</sub> and ''N''<sub>''y''</sub>. Then the following statements are equivalent:

* ''x'' ≡ ''y''
* for each open set ''U'' in ''X'', ''U'' contains either both ''x'' and ''y'' or neither of them
* ''N''<sub>''x''</sub> = ''N''<sub>''y''</sub>
* ''x'' ∈ cl{''y''} and ''y'' ∈ cl{''x''}
* cl{''x''} = cl{''y''}
* ''x'' ∈ <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''y''</sub> and ''y'' ∈ <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''x''</sub>
* <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''x''</sub> = <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''y''</sub>
* ''x'' ∈ cl{''y''} and ''x'' ∈ <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''y''</sub>
* ''x'' belongs to every open set and every closed set containing ''y''
* a [[net (topology)|net]] or [[filter (topology)|filter]] converges to ''x'' if and only if it converges to ''y''

These conditions can be simplified in the case where ''X'' is [[R0 space|symmetric space]]. For these spaces (in particular, for [[regular space]]s), the following statements are equivalent:

* ''x'' ≡ ''y''
* for each open set ''U'', if ''x'' ∈ ''U'' then ''y'' ∈ ''U''
* ''N''<sub>''x''</sub> ⊂ ''N''<sub>''y''</sub>
* ''x'' ∈ cl{''y''}
* ''x'' ∈ <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''y''</sub>
* ''x'' belongs to every closed set containing ''y''
* ''x'' belongs to every open set containing ''y''
* every net or filter that converges to ''x'' converges to ''y''

===Equivalence classes===

To discuss the [[equivalence class]] of ''x'', it is convenient to first define the [[upper set|upper]] and [[lower set]]s of ''x''. These are both defined with respect to the [[specialization preorder]] discussed above.

The lower set of ''x'' is just the closure of {''x''}:
:<math>\mathop{\darr}x = \{y\in X: y\leq x\} = \textrm{cl}\{x\}</math>
while the upper set of ''x'' is the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the [[neighborhood system]] at ''x'':
:<math>\mathop{\uarr}x = \{y\in X: x\leq y\} = \bigcap \mathcal{N}_x.</math>

The equivalence class of ''x'' is then given by the intersection
:<math>[x] = {\mathop{\darr}x} \cap {\mathop{\uarr}x}.</math>

Since ↓''x'' is the intersection of all the closed sets containing ''x'' and ↑''x'' is the intersection of all the open sets containing ''x'', the equivalence class [''x''] is the intersection of all the open sets and closed sets containing ''x''.

Both cl{''x''} and <big>∩</big>''N''<sub>''x''</sub> will contain the equivalence class [''x'']. In general, both sets will contain additional points as well. In [[R0 space|symmetric spaces]] (in particular, in [[regular space]]s) however, the three sets coincide:
:<math>[x] = \textrm{cl}\{x\} = \bigcap\mathcal{N}_x.</math>
In general, the equivalence classes [''x''] will be closed if and only if the space is symmetric.

===Continuous functions===

Let ''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y'' be a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous function]]. Then for any ''x'' and ''y'' in ''X''
:''x'' &equiv; ''y'' implies ''f''(''x'') &equiv; ''f''(''y'').
The converse is generally false (There are [[Quotient space (topology)|quotients]] of T<sub>0</sub> spaces which are [[trivial topology|trivial]]). The converse will hold if ''X'' has the [[initial topology]] induced by ''f''. More generally, if ''X'' has the initial topology induced by a family of maps <math>f_\alpha : X \to Y_\alpha</math> then
:''x'' &equiv; ''y'' if and only if ''f''<sub>α</sub>(''x'') &equiv; ''f''<sub>α</sub>(''y'') for all α.
It follows that two elements in a [[product space]] are topologically indistinguishable if and only if each of their components are topologically indistinguishable.

==Kolmogorov quotient==

Since topological indistinguishability is an equivalence relation on any topological space ''X'', we can form the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] ''KX'' = ''X''/≡. The space ''KX'' is called the '''[[Kolmogorov quotient]]''' or '''T<sub>0</sub> identification''' of ''X''. The space ''KX'' is, in fact, T<sub>0</sub> (i.e. all points are topologically distinguishable). Moreover, by the characteristic property of the quotient map any continuous map ''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y'' from ''X'' to a T<sub>0</sub> space factors through the quotient map ''q'' : ''X'' → ''KX''.  Categorically, the T<sub>0</sub> spaces form a [[reflective subcategory]] of the category of topological spaces, with the Kolmogorov quotient as the reflector.

Although the quotient map ''q'' is generally not a [[homeomorphism]] (since it is not generally [[injective function|injective]]), it does induce a [[bijection]] between the topology on ''X'' and the topology on ''KX''. Intuitively, the Kolmogorov quotient does not alter the topology of a space. It just reduces the point set until points become topologically distinguishable.
